vignette:
She is a 71-year-old woman of Oceania heritage who has spent most of her adult life in policing, and she still carries herself with the alertness of someone who has learned to read a room before she enters it. When she first begins speaking about what brought her in, she does not start with herself. She starts with her husband, with the day his health collapsed in a way neither of them expected, and with the moment her life divided into before and after.

At the time, she is still working as a police officer, already near retirement but refusing to step away. Her job has long given her a sense of structure and purpose. She knows how to keep moving when others freeze, how to stay practical when emotions run high. She has seen injury, violence, grief, and sudden loss in the course of her work, but nothing prepares her for how helpless she feels when the emergency is in her own home. Her husband is the person who has anchored her through decades of shift work, missed dinners, and the strain that police work places on family life. He is the one who has always been there when she comes home exhausted and keyed up, the one who helps her settle after a hard day. When he becomes seriously ill, she shifts immediately into action: making calls, asking questions, arranging transport, trying to hold the family together while silently believing that if she does everything right, she can keep him safe.

What follows is not one dramatic moment so much as a sequence of them. There are hospital corridors, unfamiliar smells, machines sounding in the night, and the steady erosion of her belief that things will be okay if she just stays in control. She describes sitting beside him and feeling her body become rigid, her attention narrowed to every monitor alarm and every change in his breathing. Even now, she says, she remembers the exact look on a nurse’s face when she understood the situation was worsening. That expression returns to her later at random, uninvited, as if her mind has filed it away to replay without warning.

After her husband dies, she does not fall apart in public. She organizes the paperwork, speaks clearly to medical staff, and tells relatives what they need to know. People around her often say she is strong. She has spent a lifetime being that person, so she keeps performing strength even when she feels emptied out inside. At home, though, the silence is unbearable. The routines that once marked the day become painful reminders: the chair across from hers, the kettle going on without him, the absence of his footsteps in the hall. She begins to move through the house carefully, as if she might disturb something fragile. At night, she lies awake scanning sounds, then startles at every small noise from outside. Sleep becomes light and broken, and she wakes exhausted, already tense before the day begins.

In the months that follow, she notices herself changing in ways that unsettle her. She becomes jumpy in crowded places and irritable with people who mean well but ask too much. She avoids certain conversations because they bring her too close to the hospital and to the final hours of her husband’s life. Sometimes, when she is driving to work or sitting at her kitchen table, an image comes back so vividly that she feels as though she is there again: the fluorescent lights, the urgency in the voices, the helplessness in her chest. She feels guilty for not having prevented it, even though another part of her knows there was nothing she could have done. She carries this contradiction quietly, as she has always carried difficult things quietly.

Work, once a source of steadiness, becomes harder to tolerate. She continues because that is what she has always done, but she notices that she is less patient on the job, more easily worn down by the demands of policing. She is still competent and observant, yet she is also more distant, as though part of her is watching from far away. The badge remains on her uniform, but the confidence she used to wear with it feels thinner now. At home, she often sits in silence, thinking of her husband and feeling both love and ache at once. She misses him in the small ordinary ways that hurt most, and she cannot fully rest in the present because some part of her is still waiting for the moment when everything changed.
